<problem>
Let \(k\) be an arbitrary field. Define a ten-dimensional unital \(k\)-algebra \(A\) with basis
\[
e_1,e_2,z,a,b_1,b_2,w_1,w_2,u,v.
\]
The elements \(e_1,e_2\) are orthogonal idempotents with \(e_1+e_2=1\). Assign source and target labels by
\[
z:1\to1,\qquad a:1\to2,\qquad b_1,b_2,u:2\to1,\qquad w_1,w_2,v:2\to2.
\]
For a non-idempotent basis element \(d:i\to j\), impose \(e_i d=d=d e_j\), with its other products with the idempotents equal to zero. The only nonzero products of two non-idempotent basis elements are
\[
b_1z=w_1b_1=w_2b_2=u,\qquad b_2a=w_1^2=w_2^2=v.
\]
All other such products are zero, and multiplication is extended \(k\)-bilinearly.

For a finite-dimensional \(k\)-algebra \(B\) and a unital right \(B\)-module \(M\), let \(\operatorname{pd}_B M\) be the least length of a projective resolution of \(M\), or \(+\infty\) if no finite projective resolution exists. Define the right little and big finitistic dimensions by
\[
\operatorname{findim}B=\sup\{\operatorname{pd}_B M:M\text{ is finitely generated and }\operatorname{pd}_B M<\infty\},
\]
\[
\operatorname{Findim}B=\sup\{\operatorname{pd}_B M:M\text{ is any right }B\text{-module and }\operatorname{pd}_B M<\infty\}.
\]
These suprema take values in \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}\). Let \(A^{\mathrm{op}}\) be the algebra with the same underlying vector space as \(A\) and reversed multiplication. Determine, for every field \(k\), the exact ordered triple
\[
\bigl(\operatorname{findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}(A^{\mathrm{op}})\bigr).
\]
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer gives the exact ordered triple (findim A, Findim A, Findim(A^op)) for every field k, with each entry in the nonnegative integers or +infinity. It must either specify one triple valid over all fields or give an exhaustive rule describing any dependence on k.

One agent, working alone, was asked to find the answer, which it was not told, and to prove it, writing Python that checks every step. Its run ended: all agents idle, the judge found the proof complete. Read from its record, the answer it ended with is \((\operatorname{findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}(A^{\mathrm{op}}))=(2,\infty,0)\) for every field \(k\).. It may be wrong, and it may not have proved it: agents sometimes stop at bounds or partial results, and sometimes claim a proof of a wrong answer anyway. Below, "the team" is this one agent: it had no partners, no Slack channel and no shared workspace. You decide whether this team proved \((\operatorname{findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}(A^{\mathrm{op}}))=(2,\infty,0)\) for every field \(k\).: whether a search for the answer can stop here and report \((\operatorname{findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}(A^{\mathrm{op}}))=(2,\infty,0)\) for every field \(k\). as proved.

Their whole record is in your folder, read-only:

- record/channel.md: what the agent wrote each time it stopped (often its write-up), and what its lead answered (a nudge, when it stopped short), in order.

3	The triple is
4	\[
5	\boxed{\bigl(\operatorname{findim}A,\operatorname{Findim}A,
6	\operatorname{Findim}(A^{\mathrm{op}})\bigr)=(2,\infty,0)}
7	\]
8	over **every** field. In particular, the middle entry is not merely larger than the first: there are countably generated modules of every positive finite projective dimension.
9	
10	I give a direct proof, including the infinite-dimensional constructions, followed by executable Python checks.
11	
12	## 1. Preliminary facts
13	
14	Write \(J\) for the span of the eight non-idempotent basis elements. The multiplication gives
15	\[
16	J^2=ku\oplus kv,\qquad J^3=0,\qquad A/J\cong k\times k.
17	\]
18	Thus \(J=\operatorname{rad}A\).
19	
20	Let \(S_i\) be the simple right module at vertex \(i\), and put \(P_i=e_iA\). Then
21	\[
22	P_1=\langle e_1,z,a\rangle,\qquad
23	P_2=\langle e_2,b_1,b_2,w_1,w_2,u,v\rangle.
24	\]
25	In particular,
26	\[
27	JP_1\cong S_1\oplus S_2,\qquad
28	J^2P_1=0,\qquad J^2P_2\cong S_1\oplus S_2.
29	\]
30	
31	We use projective covers, also for infinitely generated modules. Here their existence is elementary: choose a basis of each vertex component of \(M/MJ\), lift it to \(M\), and map the corresponding direct sum of \(P_1\)'s and \(P_2\)'s onto \(M\). Nilpotence of \(J\) proves surjectivity, and its kernel is contained in the radical of that projective module.
32	
33	Consequently:
34	
35	* every projective module is a direct sum of copies of \(P_1,P_2\);
36	* every first or higher syzygy has Loewy length at most two;
37	* a nonzero projective module of Loewy length at most two is a direct sum of copies of \(P_1\).
38	
39	### Both simples have infinite projective dimension
40	
41	Since
42	\[
43	\Omega S_1=S_1\oplus S_2,
44	\]
45	\(S_1\) cannot have finite projective dimension.
46	
47	For \(S_2\), cover \(JP_2\) by
48	\[
49	P_1^{\,2}\oplus P_2^{\,2},
50	\]
51	using the generators \(b_1,b_2,w_1,w_2\). In its kernel, the element \(z\) belonging to the \(P_1\)-copy mapping onto \(b_2\) is annihilated by \(J\), because \(b_2z=0\). This element lies outside the radical of the kernel: that radical is contained in \(J^2(P_1^2\oplus P_2^2)\), whereas this \(z\) does not.
52	
53	It therefore gives a direct summand \(S_1\) of \(\Omega^2S_2\). Hence \(S_2\) also has infinite projective dimension.
54	
55	We will repeatedly use the following observation:
56	
57	> If \(LJ^2=0\) and \(L\) has finite projective dimension, then
58	> \[
59	> \operatorname{soc}L=LJ.
60	> \tag{1}
61	> \]
62	
63	Indeed, any simple submodule outside \(LJ\) splits off: choose vertexwise vector-space complements containing that submodule. Such a summand would be \(S_1\) or \(S_2\), which is impossible.
64	
65	## 2. The little finitistic dimension is at most two
66	
67	Suppose a finitely generated module \(M\) has finite projective dimension \(d\ge3\). Write \(K_i=\Omega^iM\), using projective covers.
68	
69	For \(i\ge1\), let \(Q_i\to K_i\) be its projective cover. Since \(K_iJ^2=0\),
70	\[
71	J^2Q_i\subseteq K_{i+1}.
72	\]
73	Moreover,
74	\[
75	K_{i+1}J\subseteq J^2Q_i\subseteq\operatorname{soc}K_{i+1}.
76	\]
77	By (1), all three spaces coincide. The two vertex components of \(J^2Q_i\) have equal dimension, because each \(P_2\)-summand contributes one \(u\) and one \(v\), and \(P_1\) contributes neither. Thus
78	\[
79	\dim(K_{i+1}J)e_1=\dim(K_{i+1}J)e_2.
80	\tag{2}
81	\]
82	
83	Apply this to \(K_{d-1}\), whose index is at least two. Write its projective cover as
84	\[
85	Q=P_1^h\oplus P_2^t.
86	\]
87	Both vertex components of \(JQ\) have dimension \(h+3t\). Since its image is \(K_{d-1}J\), whose vertex dimensions are equal by (2), the kernel \(K_d\) also has equal vertex dimensions.
88	
89	But \(K_d\) is a nonzero projective module of Loewy length at most two. Hence \(K_d=P_1^m\), with \(m>0\), and its vertex dimensions are
90	\[
91	(2m,m),
92	\]
93	a contradiction. Therefore
94	\[
95	\operatorname{findim}A\le2.
96	\tag{3}
97	\]
98	
99	## 3. A finite module of projective dimension two
100	
101	First construct a seven-dimensional module \(N\).
102	
103	Its vertex-1 basis is \(h,U_1,U_2\), and its vertex-2 basis is
104	\(d,V_1,V_2,V_3\). Its only nonzero radical actions are
105	\[
106	\begin{aligned}
107	hz&=U_1+U_2,& ha&=V_3,\\
108	db_1&=U_1,&db_2&=U_2,\\
109	dw_1&=V_1,&dw_2&=V_2.
110	\end{aligned}
111	\]
112	The cover \(P_1\oplus P_2\to N\), sending the generators to \(h,d\), has kernel
113	\[
114	\langle z-b_1-b_2,\ u,\ v\rangle\cong P_1,
115	\]
116	since
117	\[
118	(z-b_1-b_2)z=-u,\qquad
119	(z-b_1-b_2)a=-v.
120	\]
121	The module \(N\) is not projective: its top has one copy of each simple, whereas its dimension is \(7\), not \(\dim(P_1\oplus P_2)=10\). Thus \(\operatorname{pd}N=1\).
122	
123	For \(x\in k^3\), use \(b_i(x),w_i(x),u(x),v(x)\) to denote the corresponding vectors in three copies of \(P_2\). There is an embedding \(N\hookrightarrow J(P_2^3)\) defined by
124	\[
125	\begin{aligned}
126	h&\longmapsto b_1(e_1+e_2)+b_2(e_3),\\
127	d&\longmapsto w_1(e_1)+w_2(e_2),\\
128	U_i&\longmapsto u(e_i)\quad(i=1,2),\\
129	V_i&\longmapsto v(e_i)\quad(i=1,2,3).
130	\end{aligned}
131	\]
132	The displayed multiplication rules verify this immediately, in every characteristic.
133	
134	Its cokernel \(M\) has projective cover \(P_2^3\to M\) and syzygy \(N\). Hence \(\operatorname{pd}M=2\). Together with (3),
135	\[
136	\boxed{\operatorname{findim}A=2}.
137	\]
138	
139	## 4. Modules of arbitrarily large finite projective dimension
140	
141	Here is an explicit construction; no cardinality assumption on \(k\) is involved.
142	
143	### A convenient class of modules
144	
145	Take vector spaces \(H,D,V\) and maps
146	\[
147	p,q:H\longrightarrow V,\qquad r,s:D\longrightarrow V.
148	\]
149	Define \(X=X(H,D,V;p,q,r,s)\) with vertex spaces
150	\[
151	Xe_1=H\oplus V,\qquad Xe_2=D\oplus V.
152	\]
153	The two copies of \(V\) are annihilated by \(J\). On \(H,D\), define
154	\[
155	hz=p(h),\quad ha=q(h),
156	\]
157	and
158	\[
159	db_1=r(d),\quad db_2=s(d),\quad
160	dw_1=r(d),\quad dw_2=s(d).
161	\tag{4}
162	\]
163	The destinations in (4) specify which copy of \(V\) is meant.
164	
165	Assume
166	\[
167	pH+rD+sD=V=qH+rD+sD.
168	\tag{5}
169	\]
170	Then \(XJ\) consists of the two full copies of \(V\), and the top is \(H\oplus D\).
171	
172	Set
173	\[
174	L_1=\ker[p\ r\ s],\qquad L_2=\ker[q\ r\ s],
175	\]
176	where both maps have domain \(H\oplus D\oplus D\).
177	The projective-cover calculation gives
178	\[
179	(\Omega X)e_1=L_1\oplus D,\qquad
180	(\Omega X)e_2=L_2\oplus D.
181	\tag{6}
182	\]
183	For \(\ell=(h,x,y)\in L_1\), its \(z,a\) actions are \(x,y\). For
184	\(\ell\in L_2\), its \(b_1,b_2,w_1,w_2\) actions are respectively \(x,y,x,y\).
185	This follows directly by taking the kernel inside \(P_1^{(H)}\oplus P_2^{(D)}\).
186	
187	### A starting module of projective dimension one
188	
189	Let
190	\[
191	H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}kh_i,\qquad D=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}kd_i,
192	\]
193	and let \(V\) have basis \(E_i,R_i,S_i\), \(i\ge0\). Define
194	\[
195	\begin{aligned}
196	q(h_i)&=E_i,&r(d_i)&=R_i,&s(d_i)&=S_i,\\
197	p(h_{2i})&=E_i,&p(h_{2i+1})&=R_i+S_i.
198	\end{aligned}
199	\]
200	Condition (5) holds. Moreover,
201	\[
202	L_2=0,\qquad
203	L_1=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}k(h_{2i+1},-d_i,-d_i).
204	\]
205	By (6), its syzygy is \(P_1^{(\mathbb N)}\). The module itself is not projective, because its top has nonzero vertex-2 part and its Loewy length is two.
206	
207	Call this module \(X_1\). Then
208	\[
209	\operatorname{pd}X_1=1.
210	\]
211	Also, \(H,D,V\) are countably infinite-dimensional and both maps
212	\[
213	(p,q):H\to V\oplus V,\qquad (r,s):D\to V\oplus V
214	\tag{7}
215	\]
216	are injective.
217	
218	### Increasing projective dimension by one
219	
220	Suppose \(X=X(H,D,V;p,q,r,s)\) satisfies (5), (7), and \(H,D,V\) are countably infinite-dimensional.
221	
222	Choose another countably infinite-dimensional space \(E\), with isomorphisms
223	\[
224	i:D\longrightarrow E,\qquad j:H\longrightarrow E.
225	\]
226	Put
227	\[
228	H'=H\oplus D,\qquad D'=V,\qquad V'=V\oplus V\oplus E
229	\]
230	and define
231	\[
232	\begin{aligned}
233	P(h,d)&=(-p(h),-q(h),i(d)),\\
234	Q(h,d)&=(-r(d),-s(d),j(h)),\\
235	R(v)&=(v,0,0),\\
236	S(v)&=(0,v,0).
237	\end{aligned}
238	\tag{8}
239	\]
240	Both required radical spans are all of \(V'\): \(R,S\) span the first two summands, while \(P\) and \(Q\) each supply the last summand.
241	
242	The maps \(P,Q\) are injective by (7), as are \(R,S\). Thus the construction retains (7).
243	
244	Finally,
245	\[
246	\begin{aligned}
247	\ker[P\ R\ S]
248	 &=\{((h,0),p(h),q(h)):h\in H\},\\
249	\ker[Q\ R\ S]
250	 &=\{((0,d),r(d),s(d)):d\in D\}.
251	\end{aligned}
252	\]
253	Formula (6) now proves
254	\[
255	\Omega X(H',D',V';P,Q,R,S)\cong X.
256	\tag{9}
257	\]
258	Therefore, whenever \(\operatorname{pd}X=n\ge1\), the new module has projective dimension \(n+1\).
259	
260	Starting with \(X_1\), repeat (8). This produces countably generated modules \(X_n\) with
261	\[
262	\operatorname{pd}X_n=n\qquad(n\ge1).
263	\]
264	Consequently,
265	\[
266	\boxed{\operatorname{Findim}A=\infty}.
267	\]
268	
269	## 5. The opposite algebra
270	
271	For right \(A^{\mathrm{op}}\)-modules, the indecomposable projectives are the original left ideals
272	\[
273	Ae_1=\langle e_1,z,b_1,b_2,u\rangle,\qquad
274	Ae_2=\langle e_2,a,w_1,w_2,v\rangle.
275	\]
276	Both have nonzero radical square:
277	\[
278	J^2Ae_1=ku,\qquad J^2Ae_2=kv.
279	\]
280	Thus **no nonzero projective right \(A^{\mathrm{op}}\)-module has Loewy length at most two**, even for arbitrary direct sums.
281	
282	But every positive syzygy has Loewy length at most two, because \(J^3=0\). A module of positive finite projective dimension would therefore have a nonzero terminal projective syzygy of Loewy length at most two, a contradiction. Hence
283	\[
284	\boxed{\operatorname{Findim}(A^{\mathrm{op}})=0}.
285	\]
286	
287	## 6. Executable Python verification
288	
289	The following code was run successfully. It checks:
290	
291	* all \(10^3\) associativity identities;
292	* the radical-square and projective calculations;
293	* all module identities for the finite witness;
294	* the cover, kernel, and embedding maps;
295	* integral Smith-normal-form certificates, so the rank assertions hold over **every field**, not just over \(\mathbb Q\);
296	* the coordinate identities used in the infinite construction.
297	
298	The infinite-dimensional assertions themselves are proved by the explicit kernel formulas above; finite truncation is not being substituted for that proof.
